title: \sc Remark
body_md:
Of course, we may deduce from \cite{KP2} the linear independence of
    \begin{align*}
        1, \zeta_p(3,p^{-1}), \zeta_p(5,p^{-1}), \ldots, \zeta_p(2a+1,p^{-1}),
    \end{align*}
    for large $p$. Nevertheless, since we did not particulary focus of odd values in \cite{KP2}, the condition on $p$ is much worse than the one we establish here, especially for the small values of $a$. For example, for $a=2$, we have the condition $p\geq 10^{9}$ coming from \cite{KP2}, compare to our new condition $p\geq 89$.
    Also note that the constructions established in the present paper are different from the ones of \cite{KP2}. Consequently, each of the steps described as above (linear independence, asymptotic estimates, arithmetic estimates, explicit formulas etc.) need to be done from scratch. Furthermore, all of these steps are in some sense more complicated. For example, to prove the linear independence, we manage to follow the same novel strategy developed in \cite{KP2}, however the study of the kernels of the umbral transforms is more intricate because a non-trivial residual term appears (see Section~\ref{section: det non zero} and Remark~\ref{remark: linear indpce, residual term}). \\
    Also, a striking new difficulty concerns the study of the coefficients of the expansion of the Padé approximants established in Section~\ref{section: estimates bis}. Unlike in~\cite{KP2} where there is no real difficulty in proving the integrality of the corresponding coefficients (this was essentially automatic), this is one of the most delicate points in our new constructions. We solve this issue in Section~\ref{section: estimates bis} by establishing several identities based on Zeilberger's algorithm, and then by proceeding by induction (without the integrality property, the estimates for the arithmetic of the denominator --that we believe to be almost optimal -- would have be much worse).\\
    In the case $m=6$ of Theorem~\ref{main theorem}, in order to get better asymptotic estimates, we prove that our Padé approximants satisfy some (matrix) Poincaré-Perron recurrence, which is more complex than a more usual Poincaré-Perron linear recurrence. Unlike in~\cite{KP2}, we are not dealing with an expression which is the sum of a doubly hypergeometric term, so we cannot use (the very convenient) Zeilberger's algorithm to find the recurrence. We found this matrix recurrence thanks to a handwritten Maple program.

label: pade
title: \sc Lemma
body_md:
\label{pade}
    Let $m$ be a positive integer, $f_1,\ldots,f_m\in (1/z)\cdot K[[1/z]]$ and $\boldsymbol{n}=(n_1,\ldots,n_m)\in \mathbb{N}^{m}$.
    Put $N=\sum_{j=1}^mn_j$. For any non-negative integer $M\ge N$, there exists a non-zero vector of polynomials $(P,Q_{1},\ldots,Q_m)\in K[z]^{m+1}$ satisfying the following conditions:
    \begin{enumerate}[label= (\roman*)]
      \item   \label{item: lem pade: item 1} $\deg P\le M$,
      \item  \label{item: lem pade: item 2} $\mathrm{ord}_\infty \left(P(z)f_j(z)-Q_j(z)\right)\ge n_j+1$ for $j=1,\dots,m$.
    \end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: \sc Definition
body_md:
With the notation of Lemma~\ref{pade}, fix a non-zero vector of polynomials $(P,Q_{1},\ldots,Q_m) \in K[z]^{m+1}$ satisfying the properties \ref{item: lem pade: item 1} and \ref{item: lem pade: item 2}.
    \begin{itemize}[label=$\bullet$]
      \item We say that $(P,Q_{1},\ldots,Q_m) \in K[z]^{m+1}$ is a \textsl{weight $\boldsymbol{n}$ and degree $M$ Pad\'{e}-type approximant of $(f_1,\ldots,f_m)$}.
      \item  We call the remainders, namely the formal Laurent series  $(P(z)f_j(z)-Q_{j}(z))_{1\le j \le m}$, \textsl{weight $\boldsymbol{n}$ degree $M$ Pad\'{e}-type approximations of $(f_1,\ldots,f_m)$}.
    \end{itemize}
    In the special case $n_1 = \dots = n_m = n$, we simply say that the weight is $n$.
head: environment

title: \sc Definition
body_md:
We associate to any Laurent series $f(z) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} f_k/z^{k+1}\in (1/z)\cdot K[[1/z]]$, a $K$-linear form $\varphi_f:K[t]\longrightarrow K$, called the \textsl{formal $f$-umbral transform} (or $f$-integration transform), by setting
    \begin{align*}               
        \varphi_f(t^k) = f_k \qquad (k\geq0).
    \end{align*}

label: trivial
title: \sc Lemma
body_md:
\label{trivial}
Let $g(z)\in K[[z]]$ and $\alpha\in K^\times$. The following identities hold.
 \begin{enumerate}
      \item \label{lem trivial: item 1} We have
        \[
            \mathfrak{M}^{\rm{Inv}}\left(-g\left(\dfrac{-z}{1+z}\right)\right)=\mathfrak{M}^{\rm{Inv}}(g)(-z).
        \]
        More generally, we have $\mathfrak{M}^{\rm{Inv}}(\tilde{g})(z)=\mathfrak{M}^{\rm{Inv}}(g)(z/\alpha)$, where $\tilde{g}(z)=\alpha g((1+z)^{\alpha}-1)$.
      \item \label{lem trivial: item 2}   We have $\mathfrak{M}^{\rm{Inv}}((1+z)^{\alpha}g)(z)=\mathfrak{M}^{\rm{Inv}}(g)(z+\alpha)$.
      \item \label{lem trivial: item 3}  We have $\mathfrak{M}^{\rm{Inv}}\left(-\dfrac{1}{1+z}g\left(\dfrac{-z}{1+z}\right)\right)=\mathfrak{M}^{\rm{Inv}}(g)(1-z)$.
    \end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Assertion~\ref{lem trivial: item 1} is obtained by computing $\mathfrak{M}^{\rm{Inv}}(\tilde{g})$ and noticing that $\tilde{g}(e^{z}-1)=\alpha g(e^{\alpha z}-1)$. The second assertion~\ref{lem trivial: item 2} was proved in \cite[Lemma~$5.3$]{KP2}. To get \ref{lem trivial: item 3}, we apply \ref{lem trivial: item 2} with $\alpha=-1$ and $h(z) = -g(-z/(1+z))$, and we conclude thanks to \ref{lem trivial: item 1}.

body_md:
We first prove \ref{assertion identities new}. The identities $\Theta_s(z) = \mathfrak{M}^{\rm{Inv}}(\log(1+z)^{s-1}/(z+2))$ and $\tau_1+1 = \widehat{\mathfrak{M}}^{\mathrm{Inv}}(z+2)$ together with Proposition~\ref{key prop 0}, lead to $(\tau_{1}+1)(\Theta_s) = \mathfrak{M}^{\rm{Inv}}(\log(1+z)^{s-1})$. Similarly, since $\tau_1-1 = \widehat{\mathfrak{M}}^{\mathrm{Inv}}(z)$, we obtain $(\tau_{1}-1)(R_s) = \mathfrak{M}^{\rm{Inv}}(\log(1+z)^{s-1})$. Finally, $\mathfrak{M}^{\rm{Inv}}(\log(1+z)^{s-1})= (-1)^s (s-1)!/z^s$ by \cite[Proposition~5.4]{KP}. According to \cite[Proposition~4.4]{B} and  \cite[Corollary~4.5]{B}, we have $R(z) = -R(1-z)$ and $\Theta(z) = R(z/2)-R((z+1)/2)$, from which we deduce $\Theta(z) = \Theta(1-z)$.                                                                                        
    We obtain the remaining assertions by using Lemma~\ref{lem: series expansion Theta_s and R_s} together with {Remark~\ref{Remark T,R}}.

label: poly eigen1
title: \sc Lemma
body_md:
\label{poly eigen1}
    We have the identity $V_{-1} \cap K[z] = (2z-1)V_{1}\cap K[z]$, and $\big((z+\alpha)_k(1+\alpha-z)_k\big)_{k\geq 0}$  is a basis of the space $V_{1}\cap K[z]$ for each $\alpha\in K$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Clearly $W := \left\langle (z+\alpha)_k(1+\alpha-z)_k\,;\, k\geq 0\right\rangle_{K} \subseteq V_{1} \cap K[z]$. Now, let $P(z)$ be a non-zero element of $V_{1} \cap K[z]$. Then the degree of $P$ must be an even integer $2n$. Denote by $a$ its leading coefficient and set $Q(z) = P(z) - a(z+\alpha)_{n} (1 + \alpha - z)_{n}$. Then $Q(z)\in V_{1} \cap K[z]$ and $\deg Q(z) < \deg P(z)$. We conclude by an easy induction that $P(z)\in V_{1} \cap K[z]$.

label: ans prob 1.2
title: \sc Lemma
body_md:
\label{ans prob 1.2}
    Define $U_{\pm 1} = V_{\pm 1} \cap (1/z)\cdot K[[1/z]]$. Then, $(2z-1)U_{-1} = K + U_1$ and
    \[
        U_1 = \left\{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{a_k}{(z)_k (1-z)_k} \,;\, \forall k\geq 1, a_k\in K \right\}.
    \]
head: environment

title: Proof
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Lemma~\ref{trivial}~\ref{lem trivial: item 3} implies that $(\mathfrak{M}^{\rm{Inv}})^{-1}\left(V_{1}\cap (1/z)\cdot K[[1/z]]\right)$ is equal to the space
\[
    \mathcal{V}_{1}=\biggl\{g(z)\in K[[z]] \,;\, g(z)=-\dfrac{1}{1+z}g\left(-\dfrac{z}{1+z}\right)\biggr\},
\]
in particular the modified inverse Mellin transform $\mathfrak{M}^{\rm{Inv}}$ induces a $K$-isomorphism $\mathfrak{M}^{\rm{Inv}}:\mathcal{V}_{1}\longrightarrow V_{1}\cap (1/z)\cdot K[[1/z]]$. In order to study the structure of $\mathcal{V}_{1}$, and in view of Lemma~\ref{ans prob 1.2}, we need to compute the preimages of the elements $1/((z)_{k+1}(1-z)_{k+1})$. The next result is equivalent to \eqref{eq: preimage basis of V^+}.


\begin{lemma}\label{image of M}
    For an integer $k\ge0$, we have
    \[
        \mathfrak{M}^{\rm{Inv}}\left((-1)^{k+1}\dfrac{z^{2k+1}}{(1+z)^{k+1}}\right)=\dfrac{(2k+1)!}{(z)_{k+1}(1-z)_{k+1}}.
    \]
\end{lemma}

Let $g(z)\in \mathcal{V}_{1}$ and set $f(z)=\mathfrak{M}^{\rm{Inv}}(g)(z)$. By combining Lemmas~\ref{ans prob 1.2} and~\ref{image of M}, there exists a sequence $(a_k)_{k\geq 0}$ of elements in $K$, such that
\[
    f(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{a_k(2k+1)!}{(z)_{k+1}(1-z)_{k+1}} \quad \textrm{and} \quad g(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{k+1}a_k\dfrac{z^{2k+1}}{(1+z)^{k+1}}.
\]

label: linear relations
title: \sc Proposition
body_md:
\label{linear relations}
    Let $m,n$ be positive integers and $(f_1,\ldots,f_m)\in (V_{1}\cap (1/z)\cdot K[[1/z]])^m$. Let $P(t)\in W_{1}$ with ${\rm{deg}}\,P\ge 2mn$, and define
    \[
        Q_s(z)=\varphi_{f_s}\left(\frac{P(z)-P(t)}{z-t}\right) \quad \textrm{for $1\le s \le m$.}
    \]
    The followings assertions are equivalent.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item \label{prop: pade cond: item 1} The vector $(P(z),Q_1(z),\ldots,Q_m(z))$ forms a weight $2n$ Pad\'{e} type approximants of
        $(f_1,\ldots,f_m)$.
        \item \label{prop: pade cond: item 2} $\varphi_{f_s}(t^kP(t))=0$ for $1\le s \le m \ \text{and} \ 0\le k \le 2n-1$.
        \item \label{prop: pade cond: item 3} There is a set of $n$ polynomials $\{A_k(t)\}_{k=1,3,\ldots,2n-1}$ with ${\rm{deg}}\,A_k=k$ for each odd $k$, such that
        \[
            \varphi_{f_s}(A_k(t)P(t))=0 \ \text{for} \ 1\le s \le m \ \text{and} \ k=1,3,\ldots,2n-1.
        \]
    \end{enumerate}

label: value phif
title: \sc Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that $\pi:K((1/z))\longrightarrow (1/z)\cdot K[[1/z]]$ is the projection defined in Section~\ref{section: f transform}. Since all the arguments are similar, we only prove \ref{lem value phif: item 1} and \ref{lem value phif: item 4}. Fix $j\geq 0$.  If $f(z)\in V_{1}$ (resp. $V_{-1}$) we set $P_j(z)= (z)_j(1-z)_j$ (resp. $P_j(z):=(2z-1)(z)_{j}(1-z)_j$). Then, writing $f_j(z) = P_j(z)f(z)$, we have
    \[
        \pi(f_j)=\sum_{k=j}^{\infty}\dfrac{a_k}{(z+j)_{k+1-j}(j+1-z)_{k+1-j}}\in (1/z^2)\cdot K[[1/z]].
    \]
    This implies by Proposition~\ref{key prop} (with $D = [P_j(z)]$) that $\varphi_f\left(P_j(t)\right)=\varphi_{\pi(f_j)}(1)=0$.

label: sub ker
title: \sc Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first assertion is a direct consequence of Lemmas~\ref{poly eigen1} and \ref{value phif}. According to Lemma~$\ref{ans prob 1.2}$ the exists a sequence $(a_k)_{k\geq 0}$ in $K$ such that
    \[
        f(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{a_k}{(z)_{k+1}(1-z)_{k+1}} \quad (\textrm{resp. } f(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{a_k}{(2z-1)(z)_{k}(1-z)_{k}}).
    \]
    Lemma~\ref{value phif}~\ref{lem value phif: item 3} combined with Lemma~\ref{value phif}~\ref{lem value phif: item 1} implies that
    \begin{align*}
        a_k=\varphi_f((t)_k(1-t)_{k+1}) = \varphi_f(-t(t)_k(1-t)_{k})=-\dfrac{1}{2}\varphi_f((2t-1)(t)_k(1-t)_k).
    \end{align*}
    Similarly, if $f(z)\in V_{-1}$, we conclude by using Lemma~\ref{value phif}~\ref{lem value phif: item 5} instead.

title: Proof
body_md: Since $W_{-1} = (2t-1)W_{1}$, we just have to prove that given $A(t)\in W_{1}$, the polynomial {$B(t) = \mathbf{D}_\varepsilon\big(T_n(t)^mA(t)\big)$} belongs to $T_{n-1}(t)^mW_{-1}$. Since $T_{n-1}(t)^m$ divides $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\pm 1/2}(T_n(t)^m)$, there exists $C(t)\in K[t]$ such that $B(t) = T_{n-1}(t)^m C(t)$. By \eqref{eq: basic tau pm tau stabilized subsapces}, we either have $B(t)\in W_{-1}$ and $T_{n-1}(t)^m\in W_{1}$, or $B(t)\in W_{1}$ and $T_{n-1}(t)^m\in W_{-1}$ (depending on the parity of $n$ and $m$). In both cases we conclude that $C(t)\in  W_{-1}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $\varepsilon= (-1)^{m-1}$. First, note that if $Q(t)\in W_{1}$ has degree $\geq 1$, then $\deg(\mathbf{R}_{1}(Q(t))) = \deg(Q(t))-1$. If $\deg(Q(t)) \geq 2$, then $\deg(\mathbf{R}_{-1}(Q(t))) = \deg(Q(t))-2$. This yields the expected value of $\deg(P(t))$. Let $1\le k\le 2n-1$ be an odd integer and define
    \[
        A_k(t)=(2t-1)(t)_{\tfrac{k-1}{2}}(1-t)_{\tfrac{k-1}{2}}\in W_{-1}.
    \]
    We have  $\deg(A_k(t)) = k < 2n$. Thanks to Corollary~\ref{cor key}, and since $P(t) = \mathbf{R}_{\varepsilon}^n\big(T_n(t)^m A(t)\big)$, we obtain
    \begin{align*}
        A_k(t)P(t)\in  (\boldsymbol{\tau}_{-1}+\varepsilon)(t^m K[t]) \subseteq \ker\varphi_{s}  \qquad  \text{for } k=1,3,\ldots,2n-1,
    \end{align*}
    the last inclusion coming from Corollary~\ref{kernel}. So $A_k(t)P(t)$ belongs to $\ker \varphi_s$ for $k=1,3,\ldots,2n-1$. We conclude by Proposition~\ref{linear relations}~\ref{prop: pade cond: item 3}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Given $k\ge 0$, define the polynomials
    \[
        t_{2k}(z)=\frac{(z)_k}{k!}\frac{(1-z)_k}{k!},  \qquad t_{2k+1}(z)=-\frac{(z)_{k+1}}{(k+1)!}\frac{(1-z)_k}{k!}.
    \]
    By linearity, it suffices to prove the formula when $P(z) = t_{2k}(z)$. Using \cite[(55)]{P}, we get
    \[
        \frac{t_{2k}(z)-t_{2k}(t)}{z-t} = \sum_{i=1}^{2k} (-1)^i \frac{t_{i-1}(t)}{\lfloor(i+1)/2 \rfloor} \frac{t_{2k}(z)}{t_i(z)}
    \]
    (with the notation of Prévost \cite{P}, we have $t_{i}(z) = (-1)^{\lfloor{(i+1)/2\rfloor}}N_{i}(z-1)$). By Corollary~\ref{sub ker} $(i)$, the polynomial $t_{2k}(t)$ belongs to $\ker\varphi_f$ for each $k\ge 0$, thus
    \begin{align*}                 
        \varphi_f\!\left(\frac{t_{2k}(z)-t_{2k}(t)}{z-t}\right) = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} \frac{\varphi_f(t_{2j+1}(t))}{j+1} \frac{t_{2k}(z)}{t_{2(j+1)}(z)}.
    \end{align*}
    According to Lemma~\ref{value phif} $(ii)$, we have $\displaystyle \varphi_f(t_{2j+1}(t)) = a_j \binom{2j+1}{j+1}$. To conclude, we use the identity
    \[
        \frac{t_{2k}(z)}{t_{2(j+1)}(z)} = \binom{k}{j+1}^{-2}  \frac{(z+j+1)_{k-j-1}}{(k-j-1)!} \frac{(2+j-z)_{k-j-1}}{(k-j-1)!}.
    \]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $s\in S_m$. By Theorem~\ref{Pade}~\ref{item:Thm Pade:3}, it remains to prove that $\varphi_{F_s}(C_{k}(t))=-r_{k,s}$.  Write
\[
    C_{k}(t) = \sum_{j=0}^{d_k} (-1)^j \beta_j \frac{(t)_j}{j!}.
\]
where $d_k = \deg C_k = 2(k-n+\ell)+mn$ and $\beta_j\in K$. Using the identity $\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{-1}((t)_j) = -j(t)_{j-1}$, (where $\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{-1} = \boldsymbol{\tau}_{-1}-1$), we obtain
\begin{align*}                     
    \beta_j = \mathrm{Eval}_{t=0} \circ \boldsymbol{\Delta}^j_{-1}(C_{k}(t)).
\end{align*}
On the other hand, \cite[Corollary~4.9]{KP2} (applied with $g=g_s$ and $f = F_s$), yields
\[
    \varphi_{s}\!\left(\frac{(t)_j}{j!}\right) = (-1)^{j+1} a_{s,j}.
\]
We conclude that $\varphi_{s}(C_{k}(t)) = -\sum_{j=0}^{d_k} a_{s,j}\cdot\mathrm{Eval}_{t=0} \circ \boldsymbol{\Delta}^{j}_{-1}(C_{k}(t))$.

body_md:
\label{det is const}
    Define the $M \times M$ determinant $\Omega_{m,n}$ by
    \[
        \Omega_{m,n} = \det\Big(\varphi_{s_j}\big((2t+n-1)(t)_n^m A_{k-1}(t+n/2) \big)\Big)_{1 \leq j,k \leq M}.
    \]
    There exists $c\in \mathbb{Q}^\times$ such that $\det \mathcal{M}_{m,n}(z)= c\cdot \Omega_{m,n}\in \mathbb{Q}$.

label: remark: linear indpce, residual term
title: \sc Remark
body_md:
\label{remark: linear indpce, residual term}
    Essentially, we use a method similar to the one introduced in \cite[Section~8.2]{KP2}, and whose main advantage is that it does not require to get an ``closed and explicit expression'' of the determinant. However, in the present article our arguments are more complicated because the crucial \cite[Lemma~8.4]{KP2} is now replaced by Corollary~\ref{cor: expression restricted intersection ker phi}. The main difficulty comes from the residual term $\boldsymbol{p}_{1}\big(K[t]_{\leq m-1-\delta_m}\big)$ appearing in the corollary, and which did not exist in \cite[Lemma~8.4]{KP2}. We solve this issue thanks to the technical Proposition~\ref{cor: key for non-vanishing det} of Subsection~\ref{subsection: study of kernel}.

title: Proof
body_md:
By Proposition~\ref{prop: rec coeff H^m even case} combined with Lemma~\ref{lem: rec coeff H^m even case}, we find
    \begin{align*}
        H_{n,\ell}^{(m)}(z) = (-1)^\ell H_{n,0}^{(m)}(z) U_\ell(z,n) &=  (-1)^\ell \ell!^2 \sum_{j=0}^{N^{(m)}} a_j^{(m)}(n)\frac{U_{n+j}(z)}{j!(n+j)!}\frac{U_\ell(z,n)}{\ell!^2} \\
        & = (-1)^\ell\sum_{j=0}^{N^{(m)}} a_j^{(m)}(n) \sum_{i = 0}^{\ell} b_{i}(n,j) \frac{U_{n+i+j}(z)}{(i+j)!(n+i+j)!},
    \end{align*}
    where $N^{(m)} = Mn = N_0$ and
    \begin{align*}
        b_{i}(n,j)  &= \ell!^2\frac{(n+j)!}{j!} \binom{j+\ell}{\ell-i} \binom{n+i+j}{i}\binom{n+i+j}{\ell} \frac{(i+j)!}{(n+i+j)!} \\
        &= \ell!^2\binom{j+\ell-i}{j} \binom{j+\ell}{i}\binom{n+i+j}{\ell} \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}.
    \end{align*}
    Furthermore
    \[
        \limsup_{n\to\infty} \max_{\substack{0 \leq i \leq \ell \\ 0\leq j\leq N^{(m)}}} \big\{ b_{i}(n,j)^{1/n} \big\} = 1.
    \]
    We conclude with Propositions~\ref{prop: rec coeff H^m even case} and~\ref{prop: asymptotic coeff even case}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Applying Lemma~\ref{lem: rec coeff H^m even case} with $\alpha=0$ (and noting that $k!^2S^{(0)}_k(z) = T_{2k}(z)$ for each integer $k$), we obtain, for each $N,n,j,\ell \geq $ with $n=2N$ even and $\ell \leq M \leq n$,
    \begin{align*}                                    
        \frac{T_{n+2j}(z)}{(N+j)!^2}\frac{T_{2\ell}(z)}{\ell!^2} = \sum_{i=0}^{\ell} \binom{N+j+\ell}{\ell-i} \binom{N+i+j}{i} \binom{N+i+j}{\ell}\frac{T_{n+2i+2j}(z)}{(N+i+j)!^2}.
    \end{align*}
    By Proposition~\ref{prop: rec coeff H^m odd case} combined with the above, we get
    \begin{align*}
        H_{n,\ell}^{(m)}(z) = H_{n,0}^{(m)}(z) T_{2\ell}(z)  = \sum_{j=0}^{N^{(m)}} a_j^{(m)}(n)\frac{ T_{n+2j}(z)}{j!^2}T_{2\ell}(z)= \sum_{j=0}^{N^{(m)}} a_j^{(m)}(n) \sum_{i=0}^{\ell} b_i(n,j)  \frac{T_{n+2i+2j}(z)}{(i+j)!^2},
    \end{align*}
    where
    \begin{align*}
        b_i(n,j) & = \ell!\frac{(i+j)!^2(N+j)!^2}{(N+i+j)!^2j!^2} \binom{N+j+\ell}{\ell-i} \binom{N+i+j}{i} \binom{N+i+j}{\ell} \\
        & = \binom{N+j}{\ell-i}\binom{N+j+\ell}{\ell-i} \binom{i+j}{i}^2(\ell-i)!i! \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}.
    \end{align*}
    We deduce that
    \[
        \limsup_{n\to\infty} \max_{\substack{0 \leq i \leq \ell \\ 0\leq j\leq N^{(m)}}} \big\{ b_{i}(n,j)^{1/n} \big\} = 1,
    \]
    and we conclude with Proposition~\ref{prop: rec coeff H^m odd case} and~\ref{prop: asymptotic coeff odd case}.

label: prop: estimate Pade via auxiliary seq
title: \sc Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop: estimate Pade via auxiliary seq}
    Let $x \in \mathbb{Q}$  and $m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 3}$.  For each integer $\ell= 0,\dots, M:= \lfloor (m-1)/2 \rfloor$, we have
    \[
        \limsup_{\substack{n \to \infty \\ \textrm{$n$ even}}} \max_{s\in S_m}
        \bigl\{ |P_{n,\ell}(x)|,\, |Q_{m,n,s,\ell}(x)| \bigr\}^{1/n} \le C(m),
    \]
    where $C(m)$ is defined in Theorem~\ref{thm: property of the coeff of P_n}.
head: environment
labels: prop: estimate Pade via auxiliary seq

title: \sc Remark
body_md: In Section~\ref{section: appendix rec}, we will explain how we can improve the above proposition. For $m=4$ and $m=6$, we may take $C(4) = C(6) = 1$, so that $C(m)$ can replace the constant $C_0(m)$ defined in \eqref{eq: def C(m)}.

label: thm: general rec matrix Perron
title: \sc Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm: general rec matrix Perron}
    For each $n\geq 2$, there exists a $(2M+1)\times (2M+1)$ upper triangular matrix $A(n)$, with coefficients in $\mathbb{Q}$, whose first $M$ diagonal entries are non-zero, such that, for each $s\in S_m\cup \{\infty\}$, we have
    \begin{align}\label{eq: matrix rec relation 1}
        \left(\begin{matrix}
            T_2(z)Q_{n,s,M-1}(z) \\
            \vdots \\
            T_2(z) Q_{n,s,0}(z) \\
            0 \\
            \vdots \\
            0
        \end{matrix}
        \right)
        = A(n)\left(\begin{matrix}
            Q_{n+1,s,0}(z) \\
            Q_{n,s,M-1}(z) \\
            \vdots \\
            Q_{n,s,0}(z) \\
            Q_{n-1,s,M-1}(z) \\
            \vdots \\
            Q_{n-1,s,0}(z)
        \end{matrix} \right).
    \end{align}
